title: Probabilistic Tiny Recursive Model
claim: A cheap test-time stochastic method beats deterministic baselines and much larger frontier models across several reasoning benchmarks.
layout: 3 bar-chart panels side by side, shared color legend on top, ours in red
description: A wide figure with a color legend across the top: light gray for LLM chain-of-thought, dark gray for an LLM ensemble, orange for direct prediction, blue for deterministic recursive models, and crimson for the probabilistic recursive method (ours). Below are three bar-chart panels sharing an accuracy axis. The first panel, PPBench, compares Direct, GPT-5.2, Gemini 3.1, Opus 4.6, Ensemble, TRM and PTRM. The red PTRM bar reaches 91.2, well above the 62.6 TRM bar and the 55.1 ensemble bar. The second panel, Sudoku-Extreme, shows the LLMs and Direct at 0, HRM at 55, TRM at 87.28 and PTRM at 98.75. The third panel, N-Queens, has two groups, 10x10 and 16x16, each with Direct, TRM and PTRM bars. Numbers sit above every bar, and the red PTRM label is bold. The eye goes first to the tall red bars.
caption: PTRM performance comparison. On various PPBench puzzles, PTRM ($K{=}100, D{=}48$) boosts TRM ($D{=}16$) performance by $28.6$ points without any retraining. It outperforms the strongest single frontier LLMs by $56.5$ points and an ensemble of the seven strongest LLMs (assuming a perfect verifier) by $36$ points. On Sudoku-Extreme, PTRM reaches a state of the art $98.75%$, and on N-Queens, where puzzles have many valid answers, it raises accuracy from $82.4%$ to $94.9%$ ($10{\times}10$) and from $48.1%$ to $75.5%$ ($16{\times}16$).
abstract: Tiny Recursive Models (TRM) solve complex reasoning tasks with a fraction of the parameters of modern large language models (LLMs) by iteratively refining a latent state and final answer. While powerful, their deterministic recursion can lead to convergence at suboptimal solutions, without escape mechanism. A common workaround relies on task-specific input perturbations at test time combined with answer aggregation via voting. We introduce Probabilistic TRM (PTRM), a task-agnostic framework for test-time compute scaling that addresses this limitation through stochastic exploration. PTRM injects Gaussian noise at each deep recursion step, enabling parallel trajectories to explore diverse solution basins, and selects among them using the model's existing Q head (used for early stopping in the original TRM). Without requiring retraining or task-specific augmentations, PTRM enables substantial accuracy gains across benchmarks, including Sudoku-Extreme (87.4% to 98.75%) and on various puzzles from Pencil Puzzle Bench (62.6% to 91.2%). On the latter, PTRM achieves nearly double the accuracy of frontier LLMs (91.2% vs. 55.1%) at less than 0.0001x the cost, using only 7M parameters.
